{{Short description|5th–6th century Greek mathematician}}

{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2022}}
'''Eutocius of Ascalon''' ({{IPAc-en|j|uː|ˈ|t|oʊ|ʃ|ə|s}}; {{langx|el|Εὐτόκιος ὁ Ἀσκαλωνίτης}}; {{circa}} 480s – {{circa}} 520s) was a Greek mathematician who wrote commentaries on several [[Archimedes|Archimedean]] treatises and on the [[Apollonius of Perga|Apollonian]] ''Conics''.

== Life and work ==
Little is known about the life of Eutocius. He was born in [[Ashkelon|Ascalon]], then in [[Palestina Prima]] and lived during the reign of [[Justinian I|Justinian.]] Eutocius probably became the head of the [[Alexandrian school]] following [[Ammonius Hermiae|Ammonius]], and he was succeeded in this position by [[Olympiodorus the Younger|Olympiodorus]], possibly as early as 525.<ref>Watts, p. 233-234</ref> From his testimony, it seems he traveled to other cultural centers of his time to find missing manuscripts.

Eutocius wrote commentaries on [[Apollonius of Perga|Apollonius]] and [[Archimedes]]. The surviving commentaries are:
*A [[Commentary (philology)|Commentary]] on the first four books of the ''[[Conics]]'' of Apollonius.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Conica|url=http://whistleralley.com/conics/conica/|access-date=2021-02-25|website=whistleralley.com}}</ref>
*Commentaries<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b10035288z|title=Eutocii Ascalonitae commentarius|date=1401–1500|language=EN}}</ref> on Archimedes' work:
**''[[On the Sphere and Cylinder]]'' I-II.
**''[[Measurement of a Circle|Measurement of the Circle]]'' (Latin: ''In Archimedis Dimensionem Circuli'').
**[[On the Equilibrium of Planes|''On the Equilibrium'' ''of Planes'']] I-II.
*An introduction to Book I of [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Almagest]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Eutocius – Biography|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Eutocius/|access-date=2021-10-27|website=Maths History|language=en}}</ref>
Historians owe much of their knowledge of Archimedes' solution of a cubic by means of intersecting conics, alluded to in ''On the Sphere and Cylinder'', to Eutocius and his commentaries. Eutocius dedicated his commentary on Apollonius' ''Conics'' to [[Anthemius of Tralles]], also a mathematician and the architect of the [[Hagia Sophia]] in [[Constantinople]].<ref>Boyer, p. 193. "Eutocius (born ca. 480), commented on several Archimedean treatises and on the Apollonian ''Conics''. It is to Eutocius that we owe the Archimedean solution of a cubic through intersecting conics, referred to in ''The Sphere and Cylinder'' but not otherwise extant except through the commentary of Eutocius. The commentary by Eutocius on the ''Conics'' of Apollonius was dedicated to Anthemius of Tralles (t534), an able mathematician and architect of St. Sophia of Constantinople."</ref>
